AC9EFLA06.title: Words work together to make a message
AC9EFLA06.goal: Hear how groups of words tell who or what, and what happens.
AC9EFLA06.model: Compare ‘The little dog sleeps’ with ‘Sleeps dog the little’. Which sounds like a complete message?
steps: Say ‘the little dog’ together. These words tell who the message is about.
Add ‘sleeps’ to tell what the dog does. Read the whole message aloud.
Moving the words randomly makes the message difficult to understand. Word order helps us make meaning.
AC9EFLA06.mistake: A row of familiar words does not automatically make a meaningful sentence. Say the complete message and check that the words work together.
checks: Use these words to tell a message: bird / sings / The.
Begin with the words naming the animal.
The bird sings.
Change ‘The dog sleeps’ to tell about a cat. Which word changes?
Keep the action the same.
Change dog to cat: The cat sleeps.
homework: Say a sentence about someone jumping. Draw what your sentence means.
For example, ‘The child jumps.’ Accept a meaningful spoken sentence matched by the drawing.
A sentence says ‘The frog hops.’ Which words tell who it is about, and which word tells the action?
‘The frog’ tells who; ‘hops’ tells the action.

AC9E1LA10.title: Let punctuation show the message
AC9E1LA10.goal: Choose end punctuation and use capitals for familiar names.
AC9E1LA10.model: Write ‘where is ruby’ as a question about a child named Ruby.
steps: The message asks for information, so it needs a question mark.
Start the sentence with a capital W. Ruby is a person's name and needs a capital R.
Write ‘Where is Ruby?’ Read it aloud as a question.
AC9E1LA10.mistake: Not every excited voice needs an exclamation mark. Choose punctuation to match the written message and capitalise people's names wherever they appear.
checks: Add capitals and end punctuation: ‘mia has a blue bag’.
This is a statement, and Mia is a name.
Mia has a blue bag.
Which ending fits ‘Can you help me’ — a full stop or a question mark? Explain.
Is the writer asking something?
A question mark: ‘Can you help me?’ asks a question.
homework: Write a warning using ‘Stop’ and suitable end punctuation.
Stop! An exclamation mark can show the urgent warning.
Repair ‘I played with tom.’ Explain your change.
I played with Tom. Tom is a person's name, so it starts with a capital letter.

AC9E2LA06.title: Choose the connection between two complete ideas
AC9E2LA06.goal: Join independent clauses with a conjunction that expresses their relationship.
AC9E2LA06.model: Join ‘The path was muddy’ and ‘We kept walking’ to show a contrast.
steps: Each part can stand as a sentence: The path was muddy. We kept walking.
The second idea is unexpected after the first, so ‘but’ expresses the contrast.
Write ‘The path was muddy, but we kept walking.’ Both clauses remain complete ideas.
AC9E2LA06.mistake: Adding ‘and’ does not always join two independent clauses. In ‘red and blue shoes’, it joins describing words, not two complete clauses.
checks: Join ‘I wanted to read’ and ‘The room was too noisy’ to show a contrast.
Choose a conjunction that means the ideas pull in different directions.
I wanted to read, but the room was too noisy.
Does ‘The dog barked and the gate opened’ contain two independent clauses? Name them.
Try saying each side as its own sentence.
Yes: ‘The dog barked’ and ‘the gate opened’ can each stand independently.
homework: Join ‘You can draw a map’ and ‘You can write directions’ to offer a choice.
You can draw a map, or you can write directions.
Explain why ‘birds and fish’ is not a compound sentence.
It names two groups but does not contain two independent clauses stating complete ideas.

AC9E3LA09.title: Notice information supplied by an image
AC9E3LA09.goal: Explain how an image adds meaning beyond the accompanying words.
AC9E3LA09.model: The words say ‘The picnic area is beside the creek.’ A map also marks a bridge upstream and a walking route to that bridge. What does the map add?
steps: First identify the written information: the picnic area's position beside the creek.
Read the map's symbols and route. They provide extra information about how to reach the other side.
Explain the added meaning: the map shows where to cross at a bridge, which the sentence does not tell us.
AC9E3LA09.mistake: Saying ‘the picture makes it interesting’ does not explain added meaning. Name a particular visible detail and the information it gives.
checks: A story says ‘We finally arrived.’ Its illustration shows two muddy children holding a torn map. Name information added by the image.
Use the specific details described, rather than guessing a whole backstory.
The children are muddy and the map is torn; these details suggest a difficult journey, although its exact events are not certain.
Why is ‘The map shows a bridge upstream’ stronger evidence than ‘The map is nice’?
Choose the comment that names visible information.
It identifies a specific feature and location the reader can use.
homework: Draw an image to accompany ‘The room was ready.’ Add two details that show it is ready for a birthday celebration. Label them.
For example, a birthday cake and a birthday banner. The labelled details supply the occasion not stated in the words.
Explain one meaning your image adds that the sentence alone does not give.
For example, the decorations show that the room is prepared for a birthday, rather than a lesson or meeting.

AC9E4LA11.title: Choose a synonym that fits the context
AC9E4LA11.goal: Use synonyms and antonyms precisely rather than treating related words as interchangeable.
AC9E4LA11.model: Replace ‘small’ in ‘The scientist examined a small insect’ with ‘tiny’, ‘brief’ or ‘narrow’.
steps: Identify the meaning needed: the insect's overall size.
‘Tiny’ means very small. ‘Brief’ describes a short duration; ‘narrow’ describes a small width.
Choose ‘tiny’ if the insect is very small. Read the revised sentence to check that its meaning still fits.
AC9E4LA11.mistake: Words with related meanings may differ in strength or fit different contexts. Check the whole sentence before substituting a synonym.
checks: Choose a suitable antonym for ‘generous’ when describing a person who will not share: noisy, selfish or cheerful.
Look for an opposite meaning about willingness to give.
Selfish. It contrasts with generous in this context.
In ‘a brief visit’, can ‘brief’ be replaced with ‘tiny’ without changing how natural the sentence sounds? Explain.
What does brief describe here?
No. ‘Brief’ describes a short time; ‘tiny’ normally describes size.
homework: Replace ‘walked’ with a more precise word in ‘The exhausted hikers walked slowly to camp.’ Explain the effect.
For example, ‘trudged’ suggests slow, effortful walking and fits the hikers' exhaustion.
Write a sentence using ‘bright’ to describe light, then name an antonym that fits that sentence.
For example, ‘The lamp gave a bright light.’ ‘Dim’ is an appropriate antonym here.

AC9E5LA04.title: Use sentence openings to guide the reader
AC9E5LA04.goal: Give prominence to an idea through sentence or paragraph starting points.
AC9E5LA04.model: Compare ‘Volunteers planted trees beside the oval’ with ‘Beside the oval, volunteers planted trees’. What changes in focus?
steps: Both versions report the same event.
The first begins with the people doing the work. The second first directs attention to the location.
Choose the opening that connects to the surrounding paragraph: a paragraph about the oval may benefit from placing that location first.
AC9E5LA04.mistake: A different sentence opening is not automatically better. It should connect ideas and give prominence to the intended message.
checks: A paragraph describes changes to a garden. Which opening links more directly to it: ‘In the garden, ...’ or ‘My cousin, ...’? Explain.
Look for a connection to the paragraph's current topic.
‘In the garden, ...’ directly maintains the location as the focus, unless the paragraph deliberately shifts to the cousin.
Rewrite ‘A quiet reading corner stands behind the library desk’ to give prominence to its location.
Move the location to the beginning without changing the event.
Behind the library desk stands a quiet reading corner. Other grammatical rewrites with that location first are acceptable.
homework: Write two sentences about a playground. Begin the second with a place mentioned in the first to guide the reader.
For example: ‘A new shade sail covers the sandpit. Under the sail, younger children build castles.’
Explain why your second sentence connects to the first.
It picks up a previously introduced place or feature and uses it as the starting point for new information.

AC9E6LA02.title: Separate information from the writer's judgement
AC9E6LA02.goal: Identify objective and subjective language and notice how selection can create bias.
AC9E6LA02.model: Compare ‘The trial involved 24 students’ with ‘Only 24 students bothered to take part’. What evaluation has been added?
steps: Both statements refer to 24 students taking part.
‘Only’ presents the number as disappointingly small. ‘Bothered’ suggests a judgement about people's effort or attitude.
The first uses a more neutral description. Whether 24 is adequate still depends on the investigation, not on the tone alone.
AC9E6LA02.mistake: Neutral-sounding language is not proof that a claim is true. Check the evidence and also ask what information has been left out.
checks: Replace the evaluative language in ‘The dreadful queue lasted 18 minutes’ with a neutral description.
Retain the measurable information.
The queue lasted 18 minutes.
A report includes only praise for a new canteen menu and ignores recorded complaints. How could that create bias?
Consider which perspectives readers can see.
Selecting only positive views can make support seem more universal than the evidence warrants.
homework: Write one objective and one subjective sentence about the same fictional park visit.
For example, ‘The park had three benches’ and ‘The park was wonderfully peaceful.’ The second expresses a judgement.
A headline says ‘Residents finally get a sensible crossing’. Identify two words that convey evaluation and explain them.
‘Finally’ implies an overdue change; ‘sensible’ expresses approval of the crossing.

AC9E7LA02.title: Support an evaluation with precise textual evidence
AC9E7LA02.goal: Explain a judgement about a text using a relevant feature and its effect.
AC9E7LA02.model: Evaluate the sentence ‘The gate rattled. No one answered. Then a key scraped inside the lock.’ Does it build suspense?
steps: Make a specific evaluation: the sentence sequence builds suspense.
Select evidence: brief statements delay the reveal of who is inside, and ‘scraped’ supplies an unsettling sound.
Connect the evidence to the judgement: the reader waits for an answer while noticing a sound that suggests someone is approaching.
AC9E7LA02.mistake: Retelling the events or saying ‘it is good’ does not substantiate an evaluation. Explain how an identified feature creates an effect.
checks: Which supports an evaluation of suspense more directly: ‘I like mysteries’ or ‘The writer delays revealing who holds the key’? Explain.
Look for evidence about the text itself.
The second identifies a structural choice that delays information. The first states a personal preference.
The same scene is illustrated with the gate in deep shadow. How could this support an evaluation of the mood?
Connect the visual choice to its likely effect.
The shadow conceals detail and can make the scene feel uncertain or threatening; an alternative justified reading is acceptable.
homework: Evaluate this original line using one quoted word as evidence: ‘The paper boat trembled beside the rushing drain.’
For example, ‘trembled’ makes the fragile boat seem vulnerable against the rushing water.
Revise ‘The line is effective because it is effective’ into an evidence-based judgement.
Accept a judgement naming a textual feature and explaining its effect, such as the contrast between the fragile boat and forceful water.

AC9E8LA02.title: Explain the layers in a metaphor
AC9E8LA02.goal: Use the associations of a literary comparison to explain an evaluation.
AC9E8LA02.model: A review calls an ending ‘a locked door’. How might this evaluate the story beyond saying ‘the ending is unclear’?
steps: Identify the comparison: the ending is described as a locked door.
Explore relevant associations: a barrier, withheld access and a sense that something remains on the other side.

Connect these associations to the evaluation. The reviewer may find the ending frustratingly closed, or intriguing because it invites further thought; surrounding evidence determines the stronger reading.
AC9E8LA02.mistake: Naming a metaphor does not explain its layered meaning. Link its associations to the thing being evaluated and acknowledge context.
checks: A review calls a character ‘as steady as a lighthouse’. Identify the device and explain a possible evaluative meaning.
Notice the explicit ‘as ... as’ comparison and the lighthouse's role.
It is a simile suggesting dependability or guidance, rather than literal resemblance to a building.
How does ‘the argument is a house of cards’ evaluate an argument?
Think about the structure's vulnerability.
It suggests the argument is fragile and may collapse when one part is challenged.
homework: Write a one-sentence evaluation of a fictional film using a simile, then explain the association you intend.
For example, ‘Its pace is like a bicycle with a slipping chain’ suggests uneven progress or repeated interruptions.
Why might two readers interpret ‘a locked door’ differently when evaluating an ending?
One may value clear resolution and dislike exclusion; another may value mystery. Context and evidence should support each interpretation.

AC9E9LA02.title: Distinguish a direct judgement from an implied one
AC9E9LA02.goal: Explain how allusion, evocative vocabulary or metaphor communicates evaluation indirectly.
AC9E9LA02.model: A review says ‘In this race for instant answers, the narrator chooses the tortoise's pace.’ It alludes to the fable in which a slow, persistent tortoise defeats a hare. What evaluation might be implied?
steps: Identify the allusion and the relevant source association: persistence can matter more than speed.
The review does not directly call the narrator wise or slow-witted. It frames the pace through a familiar contrast.
A plausible reading is approval of patient thought. Check nearby wording, since irony could instead make the evaluation critical.
AC9E9LA02.mistake: An allusion's meaning is not fixed by recognition alone. Explain which source association matters and how the surrounding text uses it.
checks: Compare ‘The speech was dishonest’ with ‘The speech polished every crack until nothing looked broken’. Which states its evaluation directly?
Look for the explicit judgement word.
‘Dishonest’ is direct. The second indirectly suggests concealment through the polishing metaphor.
What evaluation is suggested by describing an explanation as ‘a fog of impressive terminology’?
Connect fog to a reader's ability to understand.
The metaphor suggests obscurity: impressive vocabulary hides rather than clarifies the meaning.
homework: Rewrite ‘The ending was predictable’ as an indirect evaluation using a metaphor. Explain the implication.
For example, ‘The ending followed tracks visible from the first page’ suggests that the outcome was easy to foresee.
Why should an analysis quote the evocative wording rather than only label it ‘negative’?
The wording supplies evidence for how the evaluation is created and helps distinguish different shades of criticism.

AC9E10LA02.title: Infer values from evaluative language
AC9E10LA02.goal: Explain what an evaluation reveals about a speaker's priorities, using precise evidence.
AC9E10LA02.model: Two fictional reviewers describe the same library redesign: ‘Every metre now earns its keep’ and ‘The quiet corners have been sacrificed’. What does each value?
steps: The first uses ‘earns its keep’ to praise productive use of space, suggesting efficiency or utility is valued.
The second uses ‘sacrificed’ to frame lost quiet spaces as a significant cost, suggesting privacy or contemplative reading is valued.
These are supported inferences about priorities in these comments, not complete descriptions of either reviewer's personality. Both reviewers may hold several values.
AC9E10LA02.mistake: Do not infer a person's whole worldview from a single word. Tie a limited interpretation to the exact evaluative wording and its context.
checks: A reviewer praises a playground as ‘a place where children of every ability can join in’. Which value is foregrounded? Cite evidence.
Identify what receives approval.
Inclusion or accessibility, supported by ‘every ability’ and ‘join in’.
A review calls a building ‘beautifully untouched by fashion’. How could this reveal a value?
Consider what the praise treats as desirable.
It can suggest valuing enduring design or tradition over changing trends. The adverb ‘beautifully’ makes the approval explicit.
homework: Write two short evaluations of a fictional school garden: one prioritising food production and the other biodiversity. Use wording that reveals each priority.
For example, ‘Every bed produces a dependable harvest’ values productivity; ‘The untidy edges shelter a remarkable variety of insects’ values habitat diversity.
Explain why different evaluations of the same garden need not mean one writer has misunderstood the facts.
The writers may notice the same features but weigh them differently because their priorities differ. Factual claims still require checking.
